newsitem.title: USA: Charles Keating ordered freed on bail.
newsitem.headline: Charles Keating ordered freed on bail.

text.p: A federal judge Thursday ordered former Lincoln Savings and Loan chief Charles Keating freed on $300,000 bail, pending a decision on his request for a new trial.
U.S. District Court Judge Mariana Pfaelzer made the ruling after questioning jurors from Keating's fraud and racketeering trial three years ago, a court clerk said.
Keating's attorneys have argued that some jurors in the federal trial knew about Keating's earlier state conviction and discussed it among themselves during their deliberations.
Keating, who is serving a 12-year sentence in Tucson, Ariz., for racketeering, fraud and conspiracy, was not in court Thursday. He has 10 days to come up with the bail.
Keating became a symbol of the U.S. savings and loan crisis in the 1980's when American Continental's Lincoln Savings and Loan declared bankruptcy in 1989.

The collapse had a domino effect on America's thrift industry, as hundreds of other savings and loan institutions followed Lincoln into bankruptcy. Lincoln's failure cost U.S. taxpayers $2.6 billion, making it one of the most costly failures in U.S. history.

The decision is the latest in a string of legal setbacks to prosecutors who had portrayed Keating and his son Charles Keating III as greedy men who arranged phony land deals and bilked elderly investors out of millions of dollars.
His son is currently free on bail.

In 1993, Keating was convicted on 73 federal counts of securities and wire fraud, conspiracy and racketeeing, and ordered to pay $122 million in restitution. Two years earlier he was convicted in state court on 17 counts of defrauding investors.

However, in April, U.S. District Court Judge John Davies overturned the state convictions and ordered a new trial after determining the original trial judge gave improper instructions to the jury. The state is appealing Davies' ruling.

Last June, prosecutors suffered another defeat when Keating, 73, was granted a new hearing on the federal charges. An Appeals Court said Pfaelzer was wrong when she denied a defence motion to hold a hearing on allegations that jurors knew about the state convictions.

Pfaelzer had ruled the state convictions should not be disclosed to the jurors because it could prejudice their verdict. However, defence lawyers said at least six of the jurors knew about the state convictions.
Keating's hearing for a new trial on the federal case is scheduled for Nov. 25.
